question: MCI against cognitively normal older adults. The population class matches (Mayo Clinic Study of Aging participants for P-359's quoted figure; ADNI for P-66); the cohort difference is allowed. The shared channel is structural MRI: P-359's MCM fuses a mid-slice T1 MRI with PiB amyloid PET and concatenates MMSE, CDR, FAQ, education, gender and blood pressure; P-66 uses hippocampal and amygdala T1 ROIs (3D CNN plus radiomics) with age and sex. A multimodal model matches when the compared channel is shared (as applied in C-103).

figures.P-359: MCM-768-20, MCSA only, sagittal plane, random 85/15 train/validation split: accuracy 0.9639 (sensitivity 0.9690, specificity 0.9587). No interval printed. The class-wise rates are exact fractions of 97 (94/97, 93/97), so the evaluation set holds 194 units (187/194 = 0.9639); this does not match 15% of MCSA's 824 patients (about 124), so the unit may be scans rather than patients. Wilson, n = 194: [0.927, 0.982]; at n = 124: [0.915, 0.985]. Same table, same data and inputs: MCM-1024-20 0.7990 (Wilson [0.737, 0.849]), MCM-1536-20 0.7165 ([0.649, 0.775]); image baselines 0.65-0.74. Table 11, MCM without multi-head self-attention, sagittal best 0.7629 ([0.698, 0.817]). Pooled ADNI+MCSA+OASIS3, sagittal: 0.9492.
figures.P-66: Radiomics + 3D CNN fusion on hippocampus and amygdala, MCI vs CN, 200/200 subjects (948/853 images), five repetitions of an 80/20 image-level split: accuracy 72.7% (AUC 0.80). No interval printed. Wilson on 20% of 1801 images (n = 360): [0.679, 0.770]; at about 254 distinct test subjects: [0.669, 0.778] (derivation as in C-83).

matched_figure_check: No figure under P-66's condition exists: P-359 reports no MRI-only model and no ADNI-only result (ADNI contributes 27/27 subjects and was not assessed separately), and P-66 reports no PET or cognitive-score model. But P-359's own tables show that model configuration alone, on the same MCSA sagittal split and the same fused-image-plus-numeric inputs, spans P-66's level and the headline. MCM-1536-20, the proposed architecture with attention, scores 0.7165, and the MCM without multi-head self-attention scores 0.7629. Both lie inside P-66's interval [0.679, 0.770], and their own intervals contain 0.727. So the paper shows that the architecture and configuration difference is sufficient to produce the whole 24-point gap, which under the rule is a condition-3 failure. This follows the reading applied in C-40, where a paper's own comparators on the same input reproduced the other paper's level. C-117 left a similar within-paper ablation to the operator.
performance_validity: Not excluded on the letter: P-359's 0.9639 is below 0.97, on about 194 evaluation units, but it comes from a single random train/validation split with no separate test set and no external cohort, and it is the best of many architecture variants scored on that split (the same table has 0.72-0.89 for sibling MCM variants). P-66's image-level split can place one subject's images on both sides, which would raise, not lower, its figure.

candidate_explanations.difference: Architecture and configuration, shown sufficient within P-359: removing the multi-head self-attention module, or changing the MCM dimension, returns accuracy to P-66's range on identical data and inputs.
candidate_explanations.quote: The MCM-1024 model achieves the highest accuracy in the sagittal plane, at 76.29%.

candidate_explanations.difference: Predictor set and label circularity: P-359 feeds MMSE, CDR and FAQ (instruments used in the clinical diagnosis) and PiB amyloid PET to the classifier; P-66 uses hippocampal and amygdala MRI with age and sex.
candidate_explanations.quote: Removing cognitive test features (MMSE, CDR, and FAQ) results in the highest drop in accuracy (except for omitting motion correction and PVC in PiB-PET preprocessing)

candidate_explanations.difference: Evaluation design: one random 85/15 train/validation split, with the reported figure the best of many variants on that split.
candidate_explanations.quote: The dataset was divided into training and validation sets with a ratio of 85/15.

candidate_explanations.difference: Cohort: Mayo Clinic Study of Aging for the quoted figure against ADNI.
candidate_explanations.quote: It was nonsensical to assess the ADNI and OASIS3 separately due to their size.

reason: Both papers classify MCI against controls with MRI in the model, and the headline accuracies (0.9639 against 0.727) exclude each other's intervals. P-359 prints no MRI-only or ADNI-only result. Its own tables show that sibling configurations of the proposed model, on the same data and inputs (MCM-1536 0.7165; MCM without attention 0.7629), agree with P-66 within uncertainty in both directions. The paper therefore shows that architecture and configuration alone are sufficient for the gap, and condition 3 fails. The same reading was applied in C-40; C-117 left a similar within-paper ablation to the operator.

quotes.quote: achieves a classification accuracy of 96.3% on the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) dataset (sagittal plane), outperforming state-of-the-art models by 5%–20%.

This study integrates multiple data modalities—T1-weighted MRI, Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) PET scans, cognitive assessments such as Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) and Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), blood pressure parameters, and demographic data—to improve MCI detection.
The dataset was divided into training and validation sets with a ratio of 85/15.
We performed the same experiments with our proposed model, the only difference being that we removed the multi-head self-attention module.
it would be valuable to evaluate the individual contribution of each modality, whether imaging, clinical or demographic data, to overall model effectiveness.

In the term of MCI vs CN, radiomic-based algorithm alone obtained ACC of 71.6 % and AUC of 77.8, CNN-based algorithm obtained ACC of 69 % and AUC of 75 and their fusion showed ACC of 72.7 % and AUC of 80.
The initial step involved randomly dividing the MRI data for each classification dataset into a sizeable training and validation set (80 % of images) and a testing set (20 % of images).
